title: Are Election Laws Designed to Suppress Voting?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine voter suppression in the United States, tracing it from the Constitution's silence on voting rights and the 1789 electorate through property qualifications, the Fifteenth Amendment, Jim Crow tactics like literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Nineteenth and Twenty-sixth Amendments. They then examine whether voter fraud is real (ACORN registration fraud), and walk through eleven modern techniques: voter caging, misinformation flyers and robocalls, felon disenfranchisement, voter ID laws (including the Texas and Rice University findings), intimidating billboards and poll watchers, cutbacks to early voting and Sunday voting, off-cycle election scheduling, and ALEC-drafted model legislation. North Carolina's 2013-era laws, struck down in court, close the discussion. The episode ends with a listener mail segment featuring a fan theory connecting To Kill a Mockingbird, Go Set a Watchman and Back to the Future.

segments.title: Opening banter and framing voter suppression
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic, complain about partisan rhetoric, and describe the two sides' public justifications (voter fraud and protecting integrity) versus the alleged targeted intent behind voter suppression laws. They preview the Voting Rights Act litigation and the 2013 Supreme Court ruling.

segments.title: Who could vote in early America
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Constitution's silence on the right to vote and the 1789 presidential election, when about six percent of the population could vote. Property ownership, age and religious restrictions limited the electorate. Veterans later pushed for voting rights, and by 1850 most white men could vote.

segments.title: Reconstruction and Jim Crow suppression tactics
segments.summary: After the Civil War and the Fifteenth Amendment, Reconstruction briefly protected Black voting under federal troops. When the Union Army withdrew, Jim Crow-era Southern Democrats used literacy tests, poll taxes, a cumulative tax, and grandfather clauses to block Black voters. By 1940 only about three percent of eligible Black Southerners were registered. Similar barriers existed nationally, including residency requirements and the Chinese Exclusion Act, which barred Chinese immigrants from citizenship until 1943.

segments.title: Nineteenth Amendment, Voting Rights Act and Selma
segments.summary: Women gained the vote in 1920. Intimidation continued in the South, with Klan resurgence after federal civil rights efforts. The Selma to Montgomery march and the violent response on national television helped lead to the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which banned literacy tests. Poll taxes were banned in 1966, and the voting age was lowered to eighteen in 1971.

segments.title: Is voter fraud real? ACORN case
segments.summary: The hosts review studies, including from the Brookings Institution, finding voter fraud rare, with about eighty-six convictions over several elections, and note most convictions involved mail-in ballots that voter ID would not stop. They discuss ACORN, a community organizing group whose canvassers filed fake or duplicate voter registrations for bonuses, leading to its disbanding and to conservatives citing it as proof of fraud.

segments.title: Voter caging, misinformation flyers and robocalls
segments.summary: Voter caging involves sending undeliverable mail to voters and challenging their registrations, as in 1998 mailings to Democrats and 1981 mailings to minority voters in New Jersey, which led to a consent decree between the RNC and DNC. Misinformation flyers and robocalls giving wrong dates or telling voters they could vote by phone are hard to trace. The hosts note that such tactics are difficult to prosecute.

segments.title: Felon disenfranchisement and voter ID laws
segments.summary: Felony disenfranchisement traces to medieval civil death and spread in the US after Reconstruction. The hosts list state-by-state rules for restoring felons' voting rights and cite that about 7.7 percent of African American adults were disenfranchised versus 1.8 percent overall, and one in four Black Florida residents in 2016. They then discuss voter ID laws in thirty-two states, Texas's gun permit versus student ID distinction, and the 2005 Baker-Carter commission findings.

segments.title: Voter ID costs, Rice University study, and intimidation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the hurdles of obtaining Texas's free voter ID, such as paying forty-two dollars for a birth certificate, likened to a modern poll tax. A Rice University study found many non-voters in one Texas congressional district cited lacking ID, though most actually had it. Intimidating billboards and poll watchers, including the New Black Panther Party case in Philadelphia and the National Ballot Security Task Force, are described.

segments.title: Early voting and Sunday voting cutbacks, off-cycle elections
segments.summary: Early voting was cut in eight mostly GOP-governed states after heavy African American use in 2008. Florida and Ohio banned the Sunday before elections, affecting Souls to the Polls drives. The hosts also discuss off-cycle local elections, which they say favor organized groups such as unions, and a study by Sarah Anzia on consolidation bills.

segments.title: ALEC model voter ID bills and North Carolina law
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the American Legislative Exchange Council drafted model voter ID legislation at a 2009 meeting, which spread to states around 2010. They then describe North Carolina's law eliminating same-day registration, early voting days, out-of-precinct voting, and straight-ticket voting, and ending preregistration of high school students, which a court struck down as targeting Black voters with surgical precision. The episode closes with a discussion of Trump's voter fraud commission.
topics: North Carolina voter law struck down

segments.title: Listener mail: fan theory linking Mockingbird, Watchman and Back to the Future
segments.summary: A listener's fan theory, read by the hosts, proposes that To Kill a Mockingbird, Go Set a Watchman and Back to the Future share an alternate timeline created when Marty McFly alters events. The hosts praise it and invite listeners to send their own fan theories.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with social media and contact information and point listeners to the website for more on voter suppression.
